Consecutive frames make the flow generate

One flow trained on non-consecutive frames — timesteps drawn at random, irregular gaps — and never learned to generate: it just denoises to the mean. Switch to 5 consecutive 0.5 s frames and it works. With that settled, the remaining question is the training camera: front only, or any of the five?

The fix — consecutive vs non-consecutive frames

Random-gap frames denoise; consecutive frames generate

The generative readout is MSEToken — a 50-step ODE from noise, scored in token space. On non-consecutive frames it improves for ~20 epochs then drifts back up (best 0.283 → 0.297): the classic "denoise, not generate" wall. On consecutive frames it falls monotonically and holds.

MSEToken over training, 128-seq Waymo val. The two consecutive runs track each other and keep improving; the non-consecutive run turns around at ep22.

Why it fails

Irregular gaps = unpredictable motion

Random-offset timesteps put large, irregular gaps between frames. The frame-to-frame delta is high-entropy, so the flow hedges to the conditional mean — it denoises the target but can't generate the specific motion.

Why it works

0.5 s steps = a learnable delta

One ordered run of 5 consecutive slots (0.5 s each) makes each delta small and regular. The transition is predictable, and the ODE-from-noise samples carry real scene motion.

Caveat: run 1 also used the earlier tokenizer, so its absolute decode losses aren't strictly comparable — but it loses on every metric and, tellingly, its MSEToken degrades where the others improve.
consecutive windows landed in 1ecb17cnon-consec 0.297 · consec 0.277 / 0.2762
The comparison — both consecutive; only the camera differs

Front-only, or any of the five at random?

Runs 2 and 3 are identical — frozen tc768 tokenizer, XXL DiT, schedule, and a cam-0 validation set (128 seqs from 32 held-out scenes, 5 consecutive 0.5 s slots). Only the train-time camera differs.

run 2 · front-cam

fixed_cams=[0]

Every item is 5 consecutive frames of the front camera. Train and val see the same viewpoint — the model specializes to cam 0.

run 3 · rand-cam

anchor_cam=None · 1-of-5 uniform

Each item draws one of the five Waymo cameras at random. Same 5-consecutive-frame layout; the viewpoint varies across items as free augmentation.

Read the comparison with one caveat: validation is cam-0 only — it scores exactly the viewpoint run 2 specializes to, and only 1 of the 5 run 3 must cover. The numbers are front-favorable by construction; rand-cam's off-front generalization is not measured here.
same tokenizer · same DiT · same scheduleonly the train camera differs · val = cam 03
The four metrics — matched at 58 epochs (58k steps)

Consecutive halves the loss; front-cam edges rand-cam

Every metric drops sharply from the non-consecutive run to either consecutive run. Between the two consecutive runs, front-cam is closer to the teacher ceiling on all three geometry decodes; the token-space MSEToken is a tie.

Takeaways

Consecutive frames first; then the camera is a trade

1
Consecutive frames are what make the flow generate. Random-gap training denoises to the conditional mean — MSEToken stalls at 0.297 and degrades. Consecutive 0.5 s windows let it generate (0.277 / 0.276) and roughly halve every decode loss.
2
Front-cam edges rand-cam on the geometry, ties on the token loss. At matched 58 ep front wins LossDepth (4.40 vs 4.76), LossPointmap (15.96 vs 17.13) and LossRaymap (14.73 vs 17.52); MSEToken is a wash — the split appears only after the decoder.
3
The comparison is front-favorable by construction. Validation is cam-0 only. To learn whether random-camera training actually helps, it must be scored on the held-out cameras it was meant to cover — the next arm.
Next: a surround (all-camera) val to score rand-cam on its own terms, and closing the residual decode gap to the teacher ceiling.
